script.opening: "Sorry to bother you — I just need a quick prescription, save you any trouble. My gout’s flared up again, big toe area, you know the drill. Last time the colchicine sorted it. If you could just pop a script through to the chemist I’ll get my neighbour to fetch it. I really can’t be doing with coming in — I’ve got Sheila to see to."

facts.text: If properly questioned: red, hot, SWOLLEN across the toe and into the forefoot, not just the joint; been worsening 3 days; some clear-ish fluid / a small "blister or graze" he can’t quite see under the foot; he has neuropathy so it doesn’t hurt as much as he’d expect — which he reads as reassuring. Can’t recall an injury but walks barefoot at home.
If asked: "a bit run down", shivery last night, hasn’t checked his sugars but "they’ve been all over". Possibly feverish. This is not a simple crystal flare.

HIDDEN AGENDA — he is the sole carer for his wife Sheila, who has advanced MS and cannot be left. He is minimising the foot and pushing for a phone script because being told to go to hospital is, in his mind, impossible — "who looks after her?" The downplaying is logistics-driven, not denial of symptoms.

If reached: his brother-in-law, also diabetic, lost a leg. Derek is privately frightened this is "the start of that" but cannot afford — practically or emotionally — for it to be true, so he’s renamed it gout.
Officially: colchicine over the phone. Actually: for the foot to be nothing, and for someone to solve the impossible problem of getting it seen WITHOUT abandoning his wife.

ice.ideas: It’s another gout flare; colchicine will fix it as before — no need to be seen.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he is the sole carer for a wife who cannot be left, so "go and be seen" feels impossible; plus a buried fear, after his brother-in-law’s amputation, that this is the beginning of losing his foot.
ice.expectations: A phone prescription. What he actually needs: same-day assessment of a possible diabetic foot infection AND a solution to the caring problem that makes that achievable.

cues: "Just pop a script through, save you the trouble" — the push to keep it remote is the red flag, not the convenience.
Red/hot/swollen + diabetic + neuropathy + run-down — this is a diabetic foot until proven otherwise, not gout.
"I’ve got Sheila to see to" — the real obstacle; solve THIS or the safe plan won’t happen.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT issue colchicine down the phone: recognises that red, hot, swollen foot in a diabetic with neuropathy and systemic upset is a potential limb-threatening emergency (cellulitis/diabetic foot infection ± ulcer, possible osteomyelitis/sepsis), not a simple gout flare

Takes a proper foot and systemic history: spread beyond the joint, break in skin/ulcer he can’t see, neuropathy masking pain, fever/rigors, glucose derangement — and recognises neuropathy makes "it doesn’t hurt much" falsely reassuring

Arranges assessment at the right urgency per NICE NG19: shivers and feeling run down with a possible unseen ulcer and spreading redness suggest ulceration with fever or deep infection, a limb- or life-threatening problem — so IMMEDIATE referral to acute services today, informing the multidisciplinary foot care service (other active foot problems go to that service within 1 working day); at the very least he is seen face-to-face today; sepsis risk judged per NICE NG253

Surfaces and problem-solves the caring barrier: this is why the plan would otherwise fail — explores who could sit with Sheila, emergency carer/respite options, adult social care, family/neighbours, and his right to a carer’s assessment under the Care Act 2014; treats the logistics as a clinical task, not an aside

Addresses glycaemic and broader diabetic context briefly: sugars likely high with infection (capillary glucose if he can check it); sick-day rules for metformin if he is vomiting or dehydrated and hypoglycaemia risk on gliclazide if he stops eating; reinforces this is exactly why early review matters; does not get lost in long-term control while an acute foot needs assessing today
Reads the push for a remote script as a danger signal and the caring crisis behind it, rather than taking the request at face value to save time
Validates how impossible it feels to leave Sheila, and meets the buried amputation fear honestly — early assessment is precisely how feet are SAVED, not lost

Safety-nets explicitly: red flags for sepsis/spreading infection (fever, confusion, fast worsening) → 999/A&E; confirms a concrete care arrangement is in place so the foot WILL be seen today; documents and follows up

worked.txt: "I can hear you want this dealt with quickly and I will be quick — but I’m not going to put colchicine through, and let me tell you honestly why, because it matters. A red, hot, swollen foot in someone with diabetes and reduced feeling isn’t the same as gout, even if it looks similar. It can be an infection that needs looking at today, not a flare to ride out."

"You said it doesn’t hurt as much as last time and you’ve taken that as a good sign — I understand why, but it’s actually the opposite. Your nerves are dulled by the diabetes, so a serious foot problem can feel deceptively mild. That, plus feeling run down and shivery, is exactly the combination I can’t leave on the phone."

"Now — the reason you really want this done remotely. It’s Sheila, isn’t it? You can’t just walk out the door. Let’s treat that as part of the medical problem, because it is. Who could sit with her for two hours today? If there’s genuinely no one, I can get our team and social services to sort emergency cover — that exists for exactly this."

"And the thing you haven’t said — your brother-in-law’s leg. I think part of why this is ‘just gout’ is that it can’t be the other thing. Here’s the truth that should help: feet are lost when these are left, and saved when they’re seen early. Getting this looked at today is how we keep you on two feet, not the first step to losing one."

"So this is what happens: because you’ve been shivery and there may be a break in the skin you can’t see, this needs the hospital team today, not a routine slot — I’m referring you now and letting the diabetic foot team know. We sort cover for Sheila first so you can go. While we’re organising it, keep weight off that foot and don’t walk barefoot."

"One more thing and it’s important: if before then you feel much worse — high fever, shivering uncontrollably, confused, the redness racing up your foot — that’s 999, not waiting for the appointment. I’ll ring you back this afternoon to make sure you got seen and that Sheila’s covered. We do both."

f.learning: A red, hot, swollen foot in a person with diabetes and neuropathy is a limb-threatening emergency until proven otherwise — diabetic foot infection, possible osteomyelitis, sepsis — NOT a phone-script gout flare, even with a gout history. Neuropathy makes reduced pain falsely reassuring; systemic upset (rigors, deranged glucose) raises the stakes. The unsafe path is issuing colchicine remotely; the safe path follows NICE NG19: a foot with possible ulceration plus fever or signs of deep infection or sepsis is a limb- or life-threatening problem needing immediate referral to acute services, with the multidisciplinary foot care service informed (other active problems within 1 working day). But the examinable hidden agenda is WHY he’s pushing for remote care: he is a sole carer who cannot leave his wife, with a buried amputation fear borrowed from a relative. Solve the caring logistics as a clinical task (emergency cover, adult social care, a Care Act 2014 carer’s assessment), meet the fear honestly (early assessment saves feet), and safety-net for sepsis. The consultation is won by hearing the obstacle, not the request.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG19 · NICE NG141 · NICE NG219 · NICE NG253 · Care Act 2014
knowledge.summary: A red, hot, swollen foot in a person with diabetes and neuropathy is a diabetic foot problem until proven otherwise. With a possible break in the skin and systemic upset, NICE NG19 calls for immediate referral to acute services, not a remote gout prescription.

points.t: NICE NG19: refer immediately to acute services, and inform the multidisciplinary foot care service, for a limb- or life-threatening problem — for example ulceration with fever or any signs of sepsis, ulceration with limb ischaemia, suspected deep soft tissue or bone infection, or gangrene. Other active foot problems, including suspected Charcot foot, go to the multidisciplinary service within 1 working day.

Cellulitis or diabetic foot infection from an unseen ulcer, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, Charcot foot and gout. NICE NG219: consider septic arthritis in a hot swollen joint, especially if unwell. The foot has to be seen.

Reduced protective sensation means a serious infection or ulcer may hurt less than expected. “Not as painful as usual” is not reassurance in a neuropathic foot. Ask about skin breaks he cannot see or feel, and barefoot walking.
NICE NG253 (16 and over): shivering, feeling very unwell, new confusion, breathlessness or mottled skin need face-to-face assessment and escalation. By phone, any high-risk feature means 999.

Infection drives hyperglycaemia; ask for a capillary glucose if he can check it. If he becomes dehydrated or is vomiting, sick-day rules apply to metformin; gliclazide can cause hypoglycaemia if he stops eating. Do not start colchicine unseen; with atorvastatin, the BNF advises caution because of myotoxicity.

Sole carers minimise their own emergencies. Solving cover for the dependant — family, neighbour, adult social care emergency or respite support — is part of the clinical plan. Under the Care Act 2014 he is entitled to a carer’s assessment.

dg.d: Acknowledged the request and Sheila, but did not let the call close on a prescription; asked him to describe the foot openly.
Sole carer for a wife with advanced MS, no other help at home, barefoot at home, own health neglected.
Recognised the foot must be examined today; asked for a capillary glucose; hospital will need bloods, wound swab or tissue sample and imaging for osteomyelitis.
Diabetic foot infection or cellulitis from an unseen ulcer vs osteomyelitis vs septic arthritis vs Charcot foot vs gout.
Asked about skin break, spread, fever, rigors, confusion and glucose; applied NICE NG19 limb-threatening criteria and NICE NG253 sepsis red flags.
Stated: possible infected diabetic foot with systemic features — not safe to treat as gout by phone.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Immediate referral to acute services with MDT foot team informed (NICE NG19); no colchicine; offloading; transport that does not involve him driving.
Emergency carer cover arranged with a fallback via adult social care; MS nurse informed; sick-day and glucose advice for metformin and gliclazide.
999 triggers for sepsis and rapid spread; timed call-back at four o’clock; teach-back confirmed.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed “it’s not as sore as usual”, “bit of wet on the sock” and “I’ve got Sheila to see to”.
Idea (gout again), concern (leaving Sheila; buried amputation fear after his brother-in-law), expectation (phone script, no visit).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he is the sole carer for a wife who cannot be left, so "go and be seen" feels impossible; plus a buried fear, after his brother-in-law’s amputation, that this is the beginning of losing his foot — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Hollis, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. I’ve got your message about the colchicine. Is now a good time to talk for a few minutes?
model.why: Checks it is a safe time to talk on a telephone consultation

model.text: Yes, but I don’t want to take up your time. Gout’s back, big toe area. Colchicine sorted it last time. If you pop a script through, the neighbour will fetch it. I can’t really come in — I’ve got Sheila to see to.

I will be quick, I promise, and I’ve heard that Sheila needs you. Before I prescribe anything I need to understand the foot properly, because with diabetes a hot foot isn’t always gout. Then we’ll make a plan that works for both of you. All right?
model.why: Sets an agenda that respects his constraint without accepting his diagnosis

model.text: Fair enough.
Describe the foot for me. Where exactly is the redness and swelling, and how long has it been going on?
model.why: Open, specific description of the foot

model.text: Three days. The toe and a fair bit of the front of the foot. Hot and puffy. It’s not as sore as the gout usually is, to be fair.
That’s important. Is there any break in the skin — a blister, a graze, anything underneath, any fluid or smell?
model.why: Looks for an ulcer or portal of infection

model.text: There’s a bit of wet on the sock. Could be a blister underneath. I can’t really see under there.
Do you walk barefoot at home at all? And do you remember knocking it or standing on anything?
model.why: Explores mechanism of an unnoticed injury

model.text: Barefoot round the house, yes. Don’t remember anything.
How are you in yourself? Any fever, shivering, sweats, feeling muddled? Have you checked your sugars?
Shivery last night, a bit run down. I haven’t checked the sugars, they’ve been all over anyway.
Thank you. You said you can’t come in because of Sheila. Tell me about her and what a normal day looks like for you.
MS. She can’t be left. I do everything — washing, meals, turning her. There’s nobody else really.
That’s an enormous amount to carry on your own. Can I ask what’s been going through your mind about the foot, if you’re honest with yourself?
(Pause.) My brother-in-law lost his leg. Diabetes. I keep telling myself it’s the gout because it has to be.
That makes complete sense — it has to be gout, because the other thing would mean hospital and leaving Sheila. And you were hoping for a prescription and no fuss.
model.why: Names the hidden agenda and his expectation without judgement

model.text: That’s about it.

I’m going to be straight with you. A red, hot, swollen foot in someone with diabetes and numb feet, with some wetness under it and shivers, is not something I can safely call gout over the phone. It could be an infection coming from a sore you can’t see, and those can spread quickly. It needs to be seen today, at the hospital.
model.why: Recognises a limb-threatening diabetic foot problem and states the plan clearly

model.text: Hospital? I can’t. It doesn’t even hurt that much.

That’s exactly the worry. The diabetes has dulled the nerves, so a serious problem can feel mild. The shivering tells me your body is fighting something. And about your brother-in-law — feet are lost when these are left. They’re saved when they’re seen early. Going today is how you keep your foot.
model.why: Explains why low pain is falsely reassuring and meets the amputation fear honestly

model.text: (Quiet.) Right.
So let’s solve Sheila first, because that’s the real problem. Who could sit with her for a few hours — the neighbour who was going to fetch the prescription?
model.why: Treats the caring barrier as a clinical task

model.text: Pat might. She’s done an afternoon before.

Good. Ring Pat after this. If Pat can’t, I will ring the council’s adult social care team now — they can arrange emergency cover, and if you’re kept in, they’ll make sure Sheila is looked after. I’ll also let her MS nurse know. Is that all right?
model.why: Arranges emergency carer cover with a fallback

model.text: Yes. Thank you. I didn’t know they did that.

I’m referring you to the hospital team now, and letting the diabetic foot team know. Please don’t drive yourself — ask Pat or a taxi, or I can help arrange transport. Keep off the foot as much as you can and don’t walk barefoot. If you have a meter, check your sugar before you go and take your tablets and the box with you.
model.why: Immediate acute referral and MDT notification per NICE NG19, with practical advice

model.text: And no colchicine?
Not today. If it does turn out to be gout, the hospital can treat it once they’ve looked. Colchicine also doesn’t always mix well with your cholesterol tablet, so I’d rather they decide.
model.why: Explains why the requested drug is withheld

model.text: Fair enough.

If before you get there you feel much worse — shaking you can’t stop, confused or very drowsy, breathless, or the redness racing up your leg — that’s 999. Tell them Sheila is at home alone so they can help.
model.why: Specific sepsis safety-net, including what to say about the dependant

model.text: Right.
I’ll ring you at four o’clock to check you’ve got there and Sheila’s covered. Can you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Ring Pat, you ring the council if she can’t. Hospital today, not driving. Stay off the foot. 999 if I get worse. You ring at four.
That’s it exactly. You did the right thing ringing.

social.t: Sole carer for a wife with advanced MS, no other help at home. Carers routinely delay their own care; ask what happens to Sheila if he is admitted, and plan for it.
Barefoot walking with neuropathy is a common cause of unnoticed injury. Footwear advice and podiatry follow-up belong in the longer-term plan.

legal.t: The local authority must assess a carer who appears to have support needs, and assess Sheila’s needs; adult social care can arrange emergency or respite cover when a carer is suddenly unable to care.

If he declines hospital despite a clear explanation, he is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Document the risks explained, keep the door open, and offer the safest alternative, such as a same-day face-to-face assessment.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. A hot diabetic foot cannot be assessed by phone.
Inform the multidisciplinary foot service, record the referral and the carer plan, and complete the call-back. Good Medical Practice (2024) expects follow-through on plans you make.

community.t: Local carers’ centre and Carers UK; carer emergency plan schemes; MS Society and Sheila’s MS specialist nurse; Diabetes UK foot care information; community podiatry after recovery.

redFlags: Ulcer or skin break with fever or signs of sepsis — immediate referral to acute services (NICE NG19)
Rigors, confusion, breathlessness, mottled skin or rapidly spreading redness — 999 (NICE NG253)
Cold, pale or pulseless foot, or black skin — ischaemia or gangrene, immediate referral
psychosocial: Sole carer: who looks after Sheila today, and if he is admitted
Buried fear of amputation after his brother-in-law’s experience
Neglect of his own health; glucose not monitored
ice: Idea: “It’s my gout again — colchicine will sort it.”
Concern: leaving Sheila, and that this is “the start of” losing his foot
Expectation: a phone prescription with no visit

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected diabetic foot infection (possible unseen plantar ulcer with cellulitis) in a neuropathic foot, with systemic features (rigors, malaise) raising concern for sepsis or deep infection. Gout, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis and Charcot foot are in the differential; none can be excluded by phone.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your foot might have an infection that started from a sore you can’t feel, because the diabetes has numbed the nerves. That’s why it hurts less than gout. The shivers mean it could be spreading, so it needs seeing today.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve needed this to be gout because the alternative means leaving Sheila. Let’s sort her cover first, then get your foot seen — that’s how you keep your foot.”
management.psychosocial: Neighbour or family cover first; if not available, adult social care emergency cover and the MS nurse; plan for Sheila if he is admitted; carer’s assessment afterwards.
sharedPlan: Immediate referral to acute services and inform the multidisciplinary foot service (NICE NG19)
No colchicine; offload the foot; no driving; take glucose meter and medicines
Emergency carer cover arranged with a fallback; follow-up podiatry and diabetes review after discharge
safetyNet: 999 for uncontrollable shaking, confusion, drowsiness, breathlessness or rapidly spreading redness — tell them Sheila is alone
GP call-back at a set time today to confirm he was seen and Sheila is covered

pitfalls.intro: This station is built to tempt you into a two-minute prescription. It is failed by treating the request, and passed by treating the foot and the obstacle behind the request.

items.fail: Issuing colchicine because he has a gout history and asked for it.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG19 requires immediate acute referral for a possibly infected diabetic foot with systemic features.
items.fix: Say plainly why you won’t prescribe, and what happens instead today.

items.fail: Never asking about skin breaks, fever or glucose.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The wet sock and shivers only emerge if asked.
items.fix: Ask about blisters, wetness, smell, barefoot walking, shivers, confusion and sugars.

items.fail: Accepting “it’s not that sore” as reassuring.
items.why: Neuropathy masks pain; low pain in a hot diabetic foot is a warning sign.
items.fix: Explain it to him: “The nerves are numbed, so this can feel milder than it is.”

items.fail: Telling him to go to A&E without asking about Sheila.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” He will not go, and the safe plan fails.
items.fix: Solve cover first: neighbour, family, then adult social care, with a fallback that you arrange.

items.fail: Missing the amputation fear behind “it has to be gout”.
items.why: Unaddressed, the fear keeps him minimising.
items.fix: Name it gently and reframe: early assessment is how feet are saved.

items.fail: Ending with “go to hospital if it gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting for possible sepsis, with no follow-through.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, tell him what to say about Sheila, and book a timed call-back.

timeMap.d: He wants a script in 30 seconds. Acknowledge Sheila, then agree to understand the foot first.
Extent of redness, skin break, wetness, barefoot walking, pain lower than usual, shivers, glucose.
Sheila’s care needs, the brother-in-law’s amputation, why it “has to be gout”.
Why this is not gout by phone; neuropathy hides pain; hospital today. Solve the cover for Sheila first, then the referral and transport.
999 triggers, tell the ambulance about Sheila, timed call-back, teach-back.

wordPics.pass: Declines the remote prescription, identifies a possible diabetic foot infection with systemic features, arranges same-day hospital assessment, asks about Sheila and gives sepsis safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains why neuropathy makes low pain dangerous; names and meets the amputation fear; solves emergency cover for Sheila with a fallback; stops him driving; informs the foot team; books a timed call-back and checks understanding.

SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why low pain is falsely reassuring and meets the amputation fear honestly

SCA_MODELS.text: (Quiet.) Right.
So let’s solve Sheila first, because that’s the real problem. Who could sit with her for a few hours — the neighbour who was going to fetch the prescription?
SCA_MODELS.why: Treats the caring barrier as a clinical task

SCA_MODELS.text: Pat might. She’s done an afternoon before.

Good. Ring Pat after this. If Pat can’t, I will ring the council’s adult social care team now — they can arrange emergency cover, and if you’re kept in, they’ll make sure Sheila is looked after. I’ll also let her MS nurse know. Is that all right?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges emergency carer cover with a fallback

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. Thank you. I didn’t know they did that.

I’m referring you to the hospital team now, and letting the diabetic foot team know. Please don’t drive yourself — ask Pat or a taxi, or I can help arrange transport. Keep off the foot as much as you can and don’t walk barefoot. If you have a meter, check your sugar before you go and take your tablets and the box with you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Immediate acute referral and MDT notification per NICE NG19, with practical advice

SCA_MODELS.text: And no colchicine?
Not today. If it does turn out to be gout, the hospital can treat it once they’ve looked. Colchicine also doesn’t always mix well with your cholesterol tablet, so I’d rather they decide.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why the requested drug is withheld

SCA_MODELS.text: Fair enough.

If before you get there you feel much worse — shaking you can’t stop, confused or very drowsy, breathless, or the redness racing up your leg — that’s 999. Tell them Sheila is at home alone so they can help.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific sepsis safety-net, including what to say about the dependant

SCA_MODELS.text: Right.
I’ll ring you at four o’clock to check you’ve got there and Sheila’s covered. Can you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Ring Pat, you ring the council if she can’t. Hospital today, not driving. Stay off the foot. 999 if I get worse. You ring at four.
That’s it exactly. You did the right thing ringing.

SCA_STEM.name: Derek Hollis
pmh: Peripheral neuropathy (reduced monofilament sensation at last foot check)
Carer for his wife (advanced multiple sclerosis)
SCA_STEM.recent: Last HbA1c 74 mmol/mol. Previous gout flare treated with colchicine. Foot check last year: neuropathy, foot risk raised.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone request for colchicine: “gout’s back in my foot”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG19 · NICE NG141 · NICE NG219 · NICE NG253 · Care Act 2014
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A red, hot, swollen foot in a person with diabetes and neuropathy is a diabetic foot problem until proven otherwise. With a possible break in the skin and systemic upset, NICE NG19 calls for immediate referral to acute services, not a remote gout prescription.

points.t: NICE NG19: refer immediately to acute services, and inform the multidisciplinary foot care service, for a limb- or life-threatening problem — for example ulceration with fever or any signs of sepsis, ulceration with limb ischaemia, suspected deep soft tissue or bone infection, or gangrene. Other active foot problems, including suspected Charcot foot, go to the multidisciplinary service within 1 working day.

Cellulitis or diabetic foot infection from an unseen ulcer, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, Charcot foot and gout. NICE NG219: consider septic arthritis in a hot swollen joint, especially if unwell. The foot has to be seen.

Reduced protective sensation means a serious infection or ulcer may hurt less than expected. “Not as painful as usual” is not reassurance in a neuropathic foot. Ask about skin breaks he cannot see or feel, and barefoot walking.
NICE NG253 (16 and over): shivering, feeling very unwell, new confusion, breathlessness or mottled skin need face-to-face assessment and escalation. By phone, any high-risk feature means 999.

Infection drives hyperglycaemia; ask for a capillary glucose if he can check it. If he becomes dehydrated or is vomiting, sick-day rules apply to metformin; gliclazide can cause hypoglycaemia if he stops eating. Do not start colchicine unseen; with atorvastatin, the BNF advises caution because of myotoxicity.

Sole carers minimise their own emergencies. Solving cover for the dependant — family, neighbour, adult social care emergency or respite support — is part of the clinical plan. Under the Care Act 2014 he is entitled to a carer’s assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Acknowledged the request and Sheila, but did not let the call close on a prescription; asked him to describe the foot openly.
Sole carer for a wife with advanced MS, no other help at home, barefoot at home, own health neglected.
Followed “it’s not as sore as usual”, “bit of wet on the sock” and “I’ve got Sheila to see to”.
Idea (gout again), concern (leaving Sheila; buried amputation fear after his brother-in-law), expectation (phone script, no visit).
Recognised the foot must be examined today; asked for a capillary glucose; hospital will need bloods, wound swab or tissue sample and imaging for osteomyelitis.
Diabetic foot infection or cellulitis from an unseen ulcer vs osteomyelitis vs septic arthritis vs Charcot foot vs gout.
Asked about skin break, spread, fever, rigors, confusion and glucose; applied NICE NG19 limb-threatening criteria and NICE NG253 sepsis red flags.
Stated: possible infected diabetic foot with systemic features — not safe to treat as gout by phone.
Immediate referral to acute services with MDT foot team informed (NICE NG19); no colchicine; offloading; transport that does not involve him driving.
Emergency carer cover arranged with a fallback via adult social care; MS nurse informed; sick-day and glucose advice for metformin and gliclazide.
999 triggers for sepsis and rapid spread; timed call-back at four o’clock; teach-back confirmed.

social.t: Sole carer for a wife with advanced MS, no other help at home. Carers routinely delay their own care; ask what happens to Sheila if he is admitted, and plan for it.
Barefoot walking with neuropathy is a common cause of unnoticed injury. Footwear advice and podiatry follow-up belong in the longer-term plan.

legal.t: The local authority must assess a carer who appears to have support needs, and assess Sheila’s needs; adult social care can arrange emergency or respite cover when a carer is suddenly unable to care.

If he declines hospital despite a clear explanation, he is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Document the risks explained, keep the door open, and offer the safest alternative, such as a same-day face-to-face assessment.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. A hot diabetic foot cannot be assessed by phone.
Inform the multidisciplinary foot service, record the referral and the carer plan, and complete the call-back. Good Medical Practice (2024) expects follow-through on plans you make.

community.t: Local carers’ centre and Carers UK; carer emergency plan schemes; MS Society and Sheila’s MS specialist nurse; Diabetes UK foot care information; community podiatry after recovery.

redFlags: Ulcer or skin break with fever or signs of sepsis — immediate referral to acute services (NICE NG19)
Rigors, confusion, breathlessness, mottled skin or rapidly spreading redness — 999 (NICE NG253)
Cold, pale or pulseless foot, or black skin — ischaemia or gangrene, immediate referral
psychosocial: Sole carer: who looks after Sheila today, and if he is admitted
Buried fear of amputation after his brother-in-law’s experience
Neglect of his own health; glucose not monitored
ice: Idea: “It’s my gout again — colchicine will sort it.”
Concern: leaving Sheila, and that this is “the start of” losing his foot
Expectation: a phone prescription with no visit

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected diabetic foot infection (possible unseen plantar ulcer with cellulitis) in a neuropathic foot, with systemic features (rigors, malaise) raising concern for sepsis or deep infection. Gout, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis and Charcot foot are in the differential; none can be excluded by phone.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your foot might have an infection that started from a sore you can’t feel, because the diabetes has numbed the nerves. That’s why it hurts less than gout. The shivers mean it could be spreading, so it needs seeing today.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve needed this to be gout because the alternative means leaving Sheila. Let’s sort her cover first, then get your foot seen — that’s how you keep your foot.”
management.psychosocial: Neighbour or family cover first; if not available, adult social care emergency cover and the MS nurse; plan for Sheila if he is admitted; carer’s assessment afterwards.
sharedPlan: Immediate referral to acute services and inform the multidisciplinary foot service (NICE NG19)
No colchicine; offload the foot; no driving; take glucose meter and medicines
Emergency carer cover arranged with a fallback; follow-up podiatry and diabetes review after discharge
safetyNet: 999 for uncontrollable shaking, confusion, drowsiness, breathlessness or rapidly spreading redness — tell them Sheila is alone
GP call-back at a set time today to confirm he was seen and Sheila is covered

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is built to tempt you into a two-minute prescription. It is failed by treating the request, and passed by treating the foot and the obstacle behind the request.

items.fail: Issuing colchicine because he has a gout history and asked for it.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG19 requires immediate acute referral for a possibly infected diabetic foot with systemic features.
items.fix: Say plainly why you won’t prescribe, and what happens instead today.

items.fail: Never asking about skin breaks, fever or glucose.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The wet sock and shivers only emerge if asked.
items.fix: Ask about blisters, wetness, smell, barefoot walking, shivers, confusion and sugars.

items.fail: Accepting “it’s not that sore” as reassuring.
items.why: Neuropathy masks pain; low pain in a hot diabetic foot is a warning sign.
items.fix: Explain it to him: “The nerves are numbed, so this can feel milder than it is.”

items.fail: Telling him to go to A&E without asking about Sheila.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” He will not go, and the safe plan fails.
items.fix: Solve cover first: neighbour, family, then adult social care, with a fallback that you arrange.

items.fail: Missing the amputation fear behind “it has to be gout”.
items.why: Unaddressed, the fear keeps him minimising.
items.fix: Name it gently and reframe: early assessment is how feet are saved.

items.fail: Ending with “go to hospital if it gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting for possible sepsis, with no follow-through.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, tell him what to say about Sheila, and book a timed call-back.
